Payment Gateway vs. Payment Processor vs. Acquirer: Where Each Layer Ends
summary:
Ask three payment teams where a gateway ends and a processor begins, and you will probably get three different answers. The industry's own reference points don't settle it: the PCI Security Standards Council glossary lists ‘payment gateway' and 'PSP' as alternative names for a payment processor.
For a merchant with one provider and one market, the blur is harmless. At scale, it gets expensive. The payment gateway vs payment processor question is really a question of ownership: who holds the card data, who talks to the card schemes, who moves the money, and who pays when something goes wrong. Each answer points to a different contract, a different cost line, and a different switching cost.
Here is how we draw those lines at Corefy, where we connect merchants and payment institutions to providers across many markets, and where orchestration fits once the lines are clear.
The ownership test: what each layer actually controls
The fastest way to place any provider in your stack is to ask what it owns and who it answers to.
 





Layer
What it owns
Who it answers to
What it does not do
Payment gateway
Secure capture and transmission of payment data from the checkout
The merchant; PCI DSS as a service provider
Move funds or carry credit risk
Payment processor
Authorization and clearing messages to and from the card schemes
The acquirer, which registers it with the schemes
Sign merchants or settle funds in its own name
Acquiring bank
The merchant agreement, settlement, and financial liability
The card schemes and their financial regulator
Decide what happens to a transaction before it arrives
Payment orchestrator
Routing logic, data normalization, and reporting across providers
The merchant
Hold an acquiring license or absorb chargeback liability
 
In practice, these layers rarely arrive separately. A typical PSP contract bundles gateway, processing, and acquiring into one integration, one contract, and one invoice. That is a sensible way to start. The cost shows up later, when you want to change one layer and discover the other two come with it.

Payment gateway vs payment processor: two jobs that usually share a contract
The gateway is the merchant-facing end. It receives card data from a checkout page, app, or terminal, encrypts and forwards it. Because it handles cardholder data on someone else's behalf, PCI DSS treats it as a service provider, with the heavier compliance obligations that status carries. A gateway does not move money. You can replace it without touching your settlement arrangements, which makes it the cheapest layer to change.
The processor sits one step deeper. It converts the transaction into the message formats the card schemes expect, sends authorization requests, and handles clearing at the end of the day. Its client is usually the acquirer. Visa requires acquirers to register every third-party agent that performs services on their behalf, and the acquirer answers for them.

 
That relationship defines the processor's risk profile. A processor outage fails transactions, so its risk is operational. But the processor is not the party that pays when a merchant's chargebacks exceed its reserves.
The lines blur because vendors span layers: many gateways also process, and many processors sell a gateway. A practical test works regardless of branding: if a provider can fail your transaction but cannot be held financially liable, it sits at the gateway or processor layer.
The acquiring bank: where money and liability sit
The acquiring bank is the only layer the card schemes define. PCI SSC describes the acquirer as an entity the payment brand designates as an acquirer, bound by that brand's rules on merchant compliance. It signs the merchant agreement, assigns the merchant ID and category code, and settles funds to the merchant's account.
It also carries the liability. Visa's Acceptance Risk Standards make the acquirer responsible for overseeing its merchants and third-party agents, and for the losses they incur. Even payment facilitators, which onboard sub-merchants themselves, must partner with an acquirer that meets Visa's requirements. However many intermediaries sit in between, responsibility flows up to a licensed institution.
This is also where pricing is set. Interchange flows from the acquirer to the card issuer and, in the EU, is capped at 0.2% for consumer debit and 0.3% for consumer credit transactions. Scheme fees pass through on top. The negotiable part is the acquirer's margin and its appetite for your risk profile. When a merchant says it negotiated better processing fees, it almost always negotiated with an acquiring bank.
That makes the acquirer the one layer you cannot abstract away. You can only add more acquirers, and that's where most payment stacks start to strain.
Payment orchestration vs payment gateway: the layer above the stack
Payment orchestration vs payment gateway is the comparison I see confused most often, partly because both present to the merchant as a single API. The difference lies in where decisions are made.
A gateway connects a checkout to one processing path, or to a few paths its owner has chosen. An orchestration layer sits above gateways, processors, and acquiring banks, and connects to many of them on the merchant's terms.
In practice, that means it:
decides which provider handles each transaction, based on market, currency, card type, cost, or recent approval rates;
retries soft declines through an alternative route instead of returning a failure to the customer;
normalizes response codes, fees, and settlement data from different providers into one format;
tokenizes card data at its own layer, so stored credentials are not tied to a single provider.
What orchestration does not do matters as much. It holds no acquiring license, takes on no chargeback liability, and replaces none of the merchant agreements you hold with acquiring banks. It works on top of those contracts. We built Corefy on that premise: the merchant keeps its direct provider relationships, and the orchestration layer gives its payment team control over how they are used.
The need for that control shows in the data. In our payment maturity study of 672 businesses, 58.5% operate at a fragmented stage, running several providers through separate dashboards, reports, and processes. Single-provider dependency fell to 33.5%, and the clearest maturity signal appears at five or more providers. Connecting providers has become easy. Running them as one system has not.
The strongest objection deserves a straight answer. Orchestration adds a layer, an integration, and a vendor. For a merchant in one market with one acquirer and stable approval rates, that cost is hard to justify, and I would tell them so. The calculation changes when a second acquirer arrives, whether for redundancy, local acquiring in a new market, or a better rate. From there, payment routing, reconciliation, and provider comparison become work someone has to do. The only choice is whether it lives in custom code and spreadsheets or in infrastructure built for it.
Mapping your own stack: five questions per provider
Most payment teams know their providers by brand name. Fewer know which layer each one actually occupies. Run every provider contract through these five questions:
Whose name is on the merchant agreement? That entity is your acquirer of record, regardless of what the provider calls itself.
Which fees are pass-through and which are margin? An interchange++ breakdown shows where your cost sits; a blended rate hides it.
Who holds your stored card tokens, and can you export them? If migrating customers' cards needs the provider's cooperation, your switching cost is higher than the contract suggests.
If approval rates fall in one market, which layer would you change? If the honest answer is 'all of them, because they come as a bundle', the bundle is limiting you.
Where does your reconciliation data come from? If each provider sends settlement reports in its own format, someone on your team is doing an orchestrator's job by hand.
Final thought
Gateways, processors, and acquiring banks are defined by what they own: data in transit, messages to the schemes, and money together with its liability. Orchestration owns none of these. It owns the decision about which of them handles each payment, and that decision now shapes approval rates, costs, and resilience more than any single provider contract does.
For payment leaders, the practical step is to know where each layer in your stack ends and who controls the boundaries between them. If the answer is 'our providers', it is worth revisiting.
#paymentsDenys KyrychenkoCo-Founder & CEOCorefy26 Oct, 2026
content: Understanding the differences between payment gateways, processors, acquiring banks, and payment orchestrators is crucial for scaling businesses. Each layer dictates specific ownership, compliance, and financial liability. While bundled PSP contracts simplify early-stage operations, relying on a single provider can become expensive and restrictive over time. Properly mapping your payment stack helps control costs, improve approval rates, and reduce provider lock-in as your business expands globally.
